title: SYSK Gets Weird Playlist: The Story of the Nuclear Boy Scout
summary: Playlist rerun (number 11 of the SYSK Gets Weird playlist) of the story of David Hahn, the "Radioactive Boy Scout" from Clinton/Commerce Township, Michigan. Covers his childhood chemistry obsession, the 1963 Boy Scout Atomic Energy merit badge, his correspondence posing as a professor with an NRC isotope official, sourcing americium, radium, thorium and uranium, building a small breeder-style reactor in his mom's potting shed, the 1994 traffic stop that exposed the radioactive toolbox, the 1995 federal cleanup, his later troubled adult life and death at 39 in 2010 from combined drug effects, and the later story of Taylor Wilson. Ends with listener mail from Tiffany about her 8th-grade teacher's reading of The Jungle.

segments.title: Playlist intro
segments.summary: Chuck introduces episode 11 of the SYSK Gets Weird playlist, the story of the nuclear Boy Scout.

segments.title: Opening banter and sources
segments.summary: Hosts note the topic was suggested by David Parcher and credit Ken Silverstein, whose Harper's article and book The Radioactive Boy Scout brought the story to light, along with Natural Resources News Service journalists.

segments.title: David Hahn's family background
segments.summary: David Hahn was born in October 1976 and grew up in the Detroit suburbs. His mother Patty had mental illness and later died by suicide in 1996. He lived with his father Ken and stepmother Kathy Missig, both GM engineers, and spent weekends with his mother and her boyfriend Michael Palasek in Golf Manor.

segments.title: The Golden Book of Chemistry Experiments
segments.summary: At age 10 David received The Golden Book of Chemistry Experiments from his step-grandfather, sparking fascination with chemistry and the Curies' radium work. Within two years he was reading his father's chemistry textbooks.

segments.title: Early chemistry mishaps
segments.summary: Hosts describe David's risky early experiments: making nitroglycerin at 14, a fire at Boy Scout camp from powdered magnesium, and an overdose of canthaxanthin in a failed self-tanning attempt. His bedroom lab damage led his father to move experiments out of the house.

segments.title: Lab moves to mom's potting shed
segments.summary: After being banned from working at his father's home, David set up a lab in his mother's potting shed in Golf Manor. His father, worried about drugs, checked on him at the library and pushed him to become an Eagle Scout.

segments.title: Atomic Energy merit badge
segments.summary: David chose the Atomic Energy merit badge, introduced in 1963 with a pamphlet developed with the nuclear industry. The pamphlet included projects such as building a Geiger counter and a reactor model, which inspired David to build a real reactor.

segments.title: Neutron gun plans
segments.summary: David decided to build a neutron gun, a lead block with a cavity holding radioactive material covered in foil, aiming to start a nuclear chain reaction. The hosts say he was not trying to build a bomb.

segments.title: Posing as a professor
segments.summary: David wrote to organizations posing as Professor Han, a teacher at Chippewa Valley High School, to get materials and schematics. Despite spelling and grammar errors, adults corresponded with him enthusiastically.

segments.title: Donald Erb at the NRC
segments.summary: David's most helpful correspondent was Donald Erb, head of an NRC isotope-producing department, who unwittingly supplied him with guidance and isotopes.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Mid-episode ad break.

segments.title: Safety habits and Chippewa mascot
segments.summary: Hosts note David knew the work was dangerous; he used a lead shield, discarded contaminated clothes and kept shoes in the shed. They also joke about the Chippewa Valley mascot.

segments.title: Driving shoes tangent
segments.summary: A brief tangent about driving shoes, which David reportedly kept as his shoes for the potting shed.

segments.title: Acquiring americium and smoke detectors
segments.summary: David tried to steal americium-241 from smoke detectors at a Boy Scout camp and was sent home. He then obtained about 100 broken smoke detectors for $100 and extracted americium, which he welded with a blowtorch. The hosts explain how americium works in smoke detectors.

segments.title: Searching for uranium ore
segments.summary: David drove around Upper Michigan with a Geiger counter on his dashboard looking for natural uranium. He found pitchblende but could not purify it, so he sourced pure uranium from a Czechoslovakian firm suggested by the NRC or Donald Erb.

segments.title: Thorium from lantern mantles
segments.summary: David bought thousands of gas lantern mantles containing thorium-232 and used lithium batteries to purify it, reaching about 9,000 times natural radioactivity. He also searched junkyards and antique shops with a Geiger counter and found radium paint in an old clock.

segments.title: Neutron moderation and tritium from gun sights
segments.summary: To slow neutrons for thorium conversion, Donald Erb suggested tritium. David ordered gun sights by mail, scraped off the tritium, and had sellers re-apply it by claiming the sights were defective. He later pursued a tiny breeder reactor concept from the early 1950s.

segments.title: Breeder reactor concept and building the reactor
segments.summary: The hosts explain how breeder reactors create more fuel than they consume and why uranium-238 matters. David built a small reactor core from a blueprint in his father's textbook, combining americium, radium, aluminum shavings, beryllium and aluminum foil, which started a chain reaction.

segments.title: Reactor growth, disassembly and car stop
segments.summary: David monitored the reactor's growing radioactivity, detected it from five houses away, and disassembled it. Later police pulled him over for stealing tires and wheels, and he warned them not to open a radioactive toolbox.

segments.title: Ad break before the car search
segments.summary: Short break after the cliffhanger.

segments.title: 1994 radiological response
segments.summary: In August-September 1994 police called in a bomb squad and the federal radiological emergency response plan was triggered, involving EPA, FBI, NRC and DOE. Officials initially did not learn about the potting shed; David was 17.

segments.title: Potting shed cleanup
segments.summary: A state Department of Public Health expert later interviewed David and found the potting shed. His mother had discarded much of the material. Federal teams spent about $60,000 in June 1995 disassembling the shed and sent contaminated earth to the Great Salt Lake Desert for burial, with the remaining waste going to a local landfill.

segments.title: Aftermath and health
segments.summary: David was called Radioactive Boy at school and fell into depression. He declined EPA bodily exams. Scout leaders still awarded his Eagle Scout badge, and no one nearby appeared to suffer radiation sickness.

segments.title: Navy, Marines and adult life
segments.summary: David served in the Navy, where he was assigned to the USS Enterprise nuclear submarine but not in a nuclear role, and later joined the Marines and was honorably discharged. He attended college and later became unemployed in 2007 as his mental illness worsened.

segments.title: FBI reports and death
segments.summary: FBI records describe reports that David was off medication and using cocaine. Later complaints about stolen smoke detectors and a possible reactor did not produce evidence of new radioactive work. He was in rehab in 2010 on drug charges and died at 39 from combined alcohol, fentanyl and Benadryl, found dead in a Walmart bathroom.

segments.title: Reflections
segments.summary: Hosts reflect on David's single-minded pursuit and sad end, noting no evidence he intended harm.

segments.title: Taylor Wilson comparison
segments.summary: Taylor Wilson received the Radioactive Boy Scout book from his grandmother at age 11, later became the youngest person to achieve nuclear fusion at 14 under supervision, and became a nuclear physicist.

segments.title: Further reading
segments.summary: Hosts recommend Ken Silverstein's article and book about David Hahn.

segments.title: Listener mail from Tiffany
segments.summary: Tiffany recalls her 8th-grade social studies and reading teacher who tied The Jungle into a daily coin toss for lunch lines, and the hosts read a recited line about the chicken-labeled lamb.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank listeners for emails and note the podcast is an iHeartRadio production.
